Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

The $j$th block of $(I_n\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X)$ is $Ax_j$, which is the $j$th column of $AX$. Hence $\operatorname{vec}(AX)=(I_n\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X)$.

The $j$th column of $XB$ is $\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}b_{\ell j}x_\ell$. The $j$th block of $(B^T\otimes I_m)\operatorname{vec}(X)$ is the same sum because its $(j,\ell)$ block is $b_{\ell j}I_m$. Thus $\operatorname{vec}(XB)=(B^T\otimes I_m)\operatorname{vec}(X)$.
Adding the identities in steps 1.2 and 1.3 gives the displayed Sylvester-map representation, completing both claims.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\geq 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$, with rows and columns indexed by
$0,\ldots,n-1$ ([[def-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

For $0\leq i,j<n$, the **deleted-row-and-column matrix** $A^{(i,j)}$ is
obtained by deleting row $i$ and column $j$. The **minor** and **cofactor** at
$(i,j)$ are

$$M_{ij}(A):=\det(A^{(i,j)}),\qquad C_{ij}(A):=\varepsilon_{ij}M_{ij}(A),$$

where the sign is taken in $R$ by parity: $\varepsilon_{ij}:=1_R$ when $i+j$ is
even and $\varepsilon_{ij}:=-1_R$ when $i+j$ is odd. Writing this as
$(-1)^{i+j}$ is the usual abbreviation; it is the ring element $-1_R$ raised to
a natural-number power in $R$, not a real power. When $n=1$,
$A^{(0,0)}$ is the unique $0\times0$ matrix and its determinant is defined
locally to be $1$. For $n>1$, the determinant is the published matrix
determinant ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

The **cofactor matrix** is
$\operatorname{cof}(A):=(C_{ij}(A))$, and the **adjugate** is

$$\operatorname{adj}(A):=\operatorname{cof}(A)^{\mathsf T},$$

using the published transpose operation
([[def-ring-matrix-product-identity-and-transpose]]).

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n\ge1$, and $A\in F^{n\times n}$. The matrix $A$ is **Hurwitz** if, when its eigenvalues are considered over $\mathbb C$, every eigenvalue has strictly negative real part. For $Q,X\in F^{n\times n}$ with $Q=Q^*$, the **continuous Lyapunov equation** with coefficient $A$ and forcing $Q$ is

$$
AX+XA^*+Q=0.
$$

Here $^*$ is transpose for real matrices and conjugate transpose for complex matrices. The notations $Q\succeq0$ and $Q\succ0$ mean that $Q$ is non-negative or positive as a self-adjoint operator in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]: respectively $v^*Qv\ge0$ for all $v$, or $v^*Qv>0$ for every nonzero $v$.

Write $T=D+N$, where $D$ contains its diagonal and $N$ is strictly upper triangular. By [F3] and [F4], the exponential series is differentiable in operator norm for each finite matrix. The identity $(UTU^*)^k=UT^kU^*$ in each series term gives $e^{tA}=Ue^{tT}U^*$; [F5] gives $\|U\|_2=\|U^*\|_2=1$. Each diagonal exponential satisfies $\|e^{sD}\|_2\le e^{-\alpha s}$ for $s\ge0$.

Differentiate $e^{(t-s)D}e^{sT}$ with respect to $s$ and integrate from $0$ to $t$. Since $T-D=N$, this gives $e^{tT}=e^{tD}+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)D}N e^{sT}\,ds$. Iterating this identity produces ordered-integral terms with $k$ factors $N$ and diagonal exponentials between them. The remainder after $n$ iterations contains $n$ strictly upper-triangular factors, with diagonal factors between them and an upper-triangular exponential at the end; every nonzero matrix-entry path would have to increase its index at least $n$ times in an $n\times n$ matrix, so this remainder is zero.

The ordered simplex for $k$ integration variables has volume $t^k/k!$. By [F6], each $k$th term has norm at most $e^{-\alpha t}\|N\|_2^k t^k/k!$. Summing the terms $0\le k<n$ proves the bound for $e^{tT}$; [F5] and step 2.1 transfer it to $e^{tA}$.

$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

derivations.claim: Hessenberg reduction uses at most $\max(n-2,0)$ reflector steps. For $n\ge3$, forming one reflector costs $O(n)$ scalar operations, and applying its two-sided similarity to the remaining dense submatrix costs $O(n^2)$; summing over at most $n$ steps gives $O(n^3)$. For $n=1,2$, there are no such steps.

For an active block of size $r\ge2$, a Francis sweep has at most $\max(r-2,0)+1$ initial/chase reflectors of length two or three. Each acts on a bounded number of rows and columns across at most $n$ entries. The active block sizes sum to at most $n$, so a full sweep and its non-controller deflation/status work cost $O(n^2)$; for $n=1$ there is no active sweep. The linear sweep budgets therefore give $O(n^3)$ matrix work for the two Schur calls. The same bound covers materializing the recorded factor products: initialization contributes $O(n^3)$ and each bounded-support chase factor updates only a bounded number of dense-factor columns, at cost $O(n)$.

Each exact Schur-certificate matrix product, the transform $U^*CV$, and the final transform $UYV^*$ cost $O(n^3)$. The block substitution has at most $n^2$ block pairs; each pair sums at most $O(n)$ earlier blocks of bounded size and solves a system of dimension at most four, so all substitution work is $O(n^3)$.

Each sweep checks at most $O(n)$ active blocks, and initialization and final checks add at most $O(n)$ such calls. With $O(n)$ sweeps there are at most $O(n^2)$ sign/representation-controller calls. A bounded call executes at most $K$ instructions, giving $O(Kn^2)$ work; the fixed built-in exact polynomial tree and rational/dyadic recipe are constant-size special cases. In arbitrary-terminating mode their actual total work is precisely the additional $C_{\rm aux}$.

The reductions, sweeps, exact certificates, transforms, block sums and fixed-size solves contribute $O(n^3)$, and step 1.4 supplies the complete control contribution. Adding them gives $O(n^3+Kn^2)$ and the fixed-$K$ cubic consequence, or $O(n^3+C_{\rm aux})$ for the richer terminating route. No bound on integer bit length or bit-operation cost is used.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n\ge1$, and $A\in F^{n\times n}$. The matrix $A$ is **Hurwitz** if, when its eigenvalues are considered over $\mathbb C$, every eigenvalue has strictly negative real part. For $Q,X\in F^{n\times n}$ with $Q=Q^*$, the **continuous Lyapunov equation** with coefficient $A$ and forcing $Q$ is

$$
AX+XA^*+Q=0.
$$

Here $^*$ is transpose for real matrices and conjugate transpose for complex matrices. The notations $Q\succeq0$ and $Q\succ0$ mean that $Q$ is non-negative or positive as a self-adjoint operator in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]: respectively $v^*Qv\ge0$ for all $v$, or $v^*Qv>0$ for every nonzero $v$.

Let $A\in F^{n\times n}$ be Hurwitz and let $Q=Q^*\in F^{n\times n}$. Then the improper matrix integral

$$
X=\int_0^\infty e^{tA}Qe^{tA^*}\,dt
$$

converges and is the unique solution of $AX+XA^*+Q=0$. If $Q\succeq0$, then $X\succeq0$. If $Q\succ0$, then $X\succ0$. For $Q\succeq0$, $X\succ0$ if and only if there is no nonzero $v$ for which $e^{tA^*}v\in\ker Q^{1/2}$ for every $t\ge0$.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-continuous-lyapunov-integral-and-positivity]]: [[thm-continuous-lyapunov-integral-and-positivity]]: For Hurwitz $A$, the Lyapunov equation has a unique solution, and the integral solution is positive definite under the stated conditions.

derivations.claim: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-1$ and $-2$, so $A$ is Hurwitz by [F1]. Direct multiplication gives $BB^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $AX+XA^T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}=-BB^T$. Thus the displayed $X$ solves the balance.
For real $(u,v)$, $\begin{pmatrix}u&v\end{pmatrix}X\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}=\frac12(u+\frac23v)^2+\frac1{36}v^2$, which is positive unless $u=v=0$. Hence $X\succ0$.
Since $A$ is Hurwitz, [F2] gives uniqueness of the solution, so this positive matrix is the unique stable Lyapunov covariance-balance solution.

$$\mathcal S_{A,B}(X)=AX+XB.$$

Equip $F^{m\times n}$ with the Frobenius norm of [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. The column-vectorization isometry of [[lem-sylvester-vectorization-isometry-and-kronecker-identity]] identifies this norm with the Euclidean norm on $F^{mn}$. Define

$$\operatorname{sep}(A,-B):=\sigma_{\min}(\mathcal S_{A,B})=\min_{\|X\|_F=1}\|AX+XB\|_F.$$

Here $\sigma_{\min}$ denotes the smallest singular value of the finite-dimensional linear map under these inner products. The finite-dimensional singular value decomposition [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]] ensures this minimum is well-defined. The argument $-B$ is part of the conventional label: the operator being measured is $X\mapsto AX+XB$.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $m,n\ge1$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$ and $B\in F^{n\times n}$. Spectra of real matrices are taken over $\mathbb C$. The map $\mathcal S_{A,B}$ of [[def-sylvester-operator-and-separation-number]] is invertible if and only if

$$
\sigma(A)\cap(-\sigma(B))=\varnothing.
$$

Equivalently, for every $C\in F^{m\times n}$, the equation $AX+XB=C$ has a unique solution if and only if this spectral condition holds. The same condition is equivalent to $\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)>0$.
